subject: forest birds: multi-transect multi-year distance sampling data, 'stacked' data and pseudoreplication

messages.author: 68a511848eac9f91
messages.subject: forest birds: multi-transect multi-year distance sampling data, 'stacked' data and pseudoreplication
parts:
Hello unmarked community,

I´m totally new to distance sampling models but I have this amazing data from a bird monitoring program I´d like to use to understand more about the ecology of forest birds. I hope you can help me clarifying two very basic questions. First, the description of the data set
  • 243  3-km linear transects divided into six 500m-sections
  • abundance recorded along 3 distance bands: 0-25, 25-100, 100-1000m
  • 4 surveys a year (2 breeding season, 2 winter season). I´m just interested in breeding season so I was planning to use the max. value over the two breeding surveys for each transect-section. 
  • data collected over the period 2006-2011
I want to understand spatial variation of abundances over forested landscapes. However, my forest structure data is one for the whole period (i.e. there is not yearly variation). I´m not interested in the annual variation of abundance (so I´m not sure I need to estimate availability 'phi'  on a yearly basis; gdistsamp function, temporary emigration model Chandler et al. 2011). I  just would like to squeeze the most of the data I have for the period the forest structure data was built.

I´ve looked through other questions in this group and I found something similar from 2016!
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/unmarked/DvliCEn91BI  
where Andy recommended using the gdistsamp function with 'stacked' data structure. I think this will work for my case too but...

My questions here are,
  • how should I deal with yearly 'pseudoreplication'? (would adding a factor(year) as a predictor among the abundance covariates suffice?)
  • would it make sense at all to use all the abundance data for the 6 years (2006-2011) when I only have one estimate of forest landscape and structure for the whole period?
  • how could I incorporate in the model the potential autocorrelation between abundance values along the six sections of each linear transect? (I understand the model does not accept a random effect for the transect. I guess I could add the transect as a fixed effect but it has 243 levels!). Is looking for autocorrelation in residuals the only thing I can do?
Many thanks for your reading until here and your help
Best,
Ale

messages.author: 0c8e4d9395a2aae5
messages.subject: Re: forest birds: multi-transect multi-year distance sampling data, 'stacked' data and pseudoreplication
parts:
Alejandra,

First, I wouldn't dismiss the temporary emigration model.  I think your approach is fine, but you may be more fully taking advantage of your two surveys with gmultmix.

Your question on stacking data has been covered a lot in this group.  Last I read, it appeared to be generally acceptable as long as you used the year covariate.

To account for spatial autocorrelation, one approach is to add a covariate for densities in adjacent transects or sections (i.e. autologistic regression); see here for more direction: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/unmarked/KYrrgnxVzAg/Srm9UqXkz3QJ.

Regarding using one measure of forest structure, 6 years seems like a long time--you'd need to assume that there was no significant disturbance or succession or management. Repeat structure measures from a subset of transects would be useful.  But with the size of your dataset, I wonder if it's necessary to push that assumption, as you'd have good numbers for many bird species in even a single year.  Estimating spatial and temporal trends using data across the full timeframe, regardless of structure/landscape variables, would likely be useful.


-Mike Worland

Hi Mike,

Many many thanks for your quick and thorough reply,

Regarding the forest structure: I don´t think I didn´t explain myself well in my previous post. The forest structure data I have was derived from LIDAR data taken over the whole study area where my sampling transects are scattered (approx. 32,000 km2) between 2002 -2011 (different parts of the region were covered by LIDAR flights over that period but I don´t know exactly when a particular area was flown).  The combination of LIDAR data with ground truth measurements of forest structure from national forest inventory plots was used to generate a set of spatially continuous layers of forest structure indicators over the study area (canopy cover,  basal area, etc.; 20 m resolution). This is the only information available so the only assumption I can make is that the forest structure is constant over 2002-2011. 

That´s why I was thinking of making the most of the bird data that matches the time frame the forest structure data was developed (2006 -2011). This will allow capturing temporal abundance fluctuations within a given time window. While, I cannot link those fluctuations to changes in forest management, composition or structure in each transect,  I seek to assess whether differences in abundance over space can be linked to differences in forest properties (taking advantage of having my transects scattered across the entire region: a space for time evaluation).

Does my approach still make sense?

Thanks again,

Alejandra

messages.author: 0c8e4d9395a2aae5
messages.subject: Re: forest birds: multi-transect multi-year distance sampling data, 'stacked' data and pseudoreplication
parts:
Alejandra, your question is more of a forest ecology question than an unmarked question, so certainly worth getting input from others.  I think you can make the case it's an appropriate approach given the generality of your forest measures, again as long as there wasn't a major disturbance in the area (like widespread logging or windthrow).  My guess is if the Lidar didn't capture the forest structure in some spots because of disturbance or whatever, then this would lead to additional error in your associations rather than biased, misleading associations.  I think the analysis would be worthwhile.  Best of luck on this.

Mike Worland
